items.title: L10: Weighing competing offers and opportunities
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: When two offers or opportunities compete, the decision is a judgement among trade-offs, not a search for a perfect option. Start by identifying what matters most to you over the next three to five years: skills, grade progression, pay, location, working pattern, the quality of line management, job security and the fit with your values. Then compare each option on those factors, using evidence rather than the impression given at interview. Ask questions that reveal substance: who you would report to, how the team is performing, what development support exists, how many people have progressed from the role, and what a typical week looks like. For a fixed-term post, ask about the likelihood of extension. For a promotion offer, ask how support during the first months is arranged. Take care with short-term gains: a higher salary in a role with limited scope can cost more in lost development than it gains. Equally, a prestigious department may give less hands-on responsibility than a smaller one. Consider reversibility: which option can you leave or change more easily if it does not work? Weigh the risk of delay too: waiting for a better option can mean losing a good one. Whatever you decide, respond to each department within its deadline, thank the one you decline, and keep the relationship positive, since you may meet the people again. Avoid playing one department against another by exaggeration. If the offers are close, trust the factors you ranked highest, and accept that no choice is certain.

questions.prompt: Two offers are close in pay and grade. Which comparison would best reveal how the roles differ?

options.text: Which department has the larger headquarters building and more senior visitors
Which interview panel was larger and so had more experience
Which offer letter arrived first and was most promptly issued
Who you would report to, what development exists and what a week involves

questions.hint: Substance about the work and support shows the real difference.

questions.prompt: Why can a higher salary in a role with limited scope be a poor choice?

options.text: The development lost can outweigh the extra pay over a few years
Higher salaries are taxed more heavily in the Civil Service than lower ones
The extra pay is normally withdrawn once probation has ended
Roles with limited scope always carry longer notice periods

questions.hint: Long-term development can matter more than a small pay difference.

questions.prompt: Which question about a fixed-term post is most useful?

options.text: How many fixed-term posts the department held last year
How likely extension or permanency is, and on what basis
Whether fixed-term staff get the same annual pay award
Whether the department prefers fixed-term staff for later permanent posts

questions.hint: The likelihood of continuation is central to the risk.

questions.prompt: What does considering 'reversibility' mean in choosing between offers?

options.text: Asking whether the department could reverse its offer after acceptance
Choosing the option with the shorter notice period so you can be released sooner
Asking which option you could leave or change more easily if it does not work
Choosing the option that pays less so that any refund is easier

questions.hint: A reversible choice reduces the cost of being wrong.

questions.prompt: A candidate delays an acceptable offer to wait for a preferred role that has not yet reached interview. What is the main risk?

options.text: Pre-employment checks must be started again from the beginning
The department withdraws the application for the preferred role
The preferred role is automatically given to another candidate
The acceptable offer may lapse and the other never come

questions.hint: Waiting carries the risk of losing a good option for an uncertain one.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate treat the department whose offer they decline?

options.text: Explain that the other offer is better in every respect
Say nothing, since declining is a private decision for the candidate
Respond within the deadline and thank them
Ask them to hold the offer open in case the other falls through

questions.hint: You may meet the same people again, and courtesy costs nothing.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour is improper when choosing between two departments?

options.text: Asking for a short extension to decide, giving a reason
Exaggerating one offer to pressure the other
Telling each department when a reply will be sent
Asking each department for the information needed to decide

questions.hint: Misstating a situation to gain advantage is dishonest.

questions.prompt: A prestigious department offers less hands-on responsibility than a smaller one. What is the sensible way to weigh this?

options.text: Judge each by the scope and evidence it would build, not only by reputation
Always choose the smaller department, since scope outweighs everything else
Always choose the larger department, since its reputation outweighs scope
Choose whichever has the more impressive job title

questions.hint: Reputation and scope are both relevant; evidence value matters.

questions.prompt: When two offers are very close, what is a reasonable way to decide?

options.text: Choose the offer that arrived last, as its terms are newer
Ask each department to rank its own offer against the other
Toss a coin so that regret is avoided afterwards
Rely on your highest-ranked factors, accepting uncertainty

questions.hint: Close decisions rest on your own priorities.

questions.prompt: Why should a candidate ask about how many people have progressed from a role?

options.text: It tells you how many candidates applied for the post
It reveals the preferences of the interview panel
It shows whether the role leads anywhere
It shows the pay for the next grade up in the profession

questions.hint: Progression history is evidence of development value.

items.title: L10: Inside knowledge, confidentiality and open competition
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles
items.body: Civil servants often have access to information that candidates outside do not, such as workforce plans, budgets, restructures and unadvertised posts. The Civil Service Code requires integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality, and part of integrity is not misusing official information for personal gain. This has practical effects in recruitment. If you know that a post is planned, you should not tell a friend or relative before it is advertised, and you should not use the information to prepare an application if that gives you an advantage that others cannot have, unless the information will be public at the same time. If you are involved in designing a post, you should not shape its criteria to fit a particular person. If you sit on a panel, you must not discuss candidates outside the process, and you should not use what you know about a candidate from other work to supplement the evidence given in the application, unless the process permits it. Where you hold relevant knowledge that is not in the application, the fairest approach is to declare it and let the chair decide how to proceed. After a competition, the results and notes are confidential, and you should not share them with unsuccessful candidates or their managers. These rules protect both candidates and the Service's reputation. They also protect individuals, because an appointment that is later shown to have been made with unfair advantage can be challenged and the people involved may face disciplinary action. When in doubt, ask HR or a nominated officer before acting.

questions.prompt: Mira works in a team planning a restructure and knows that a new EO post will be advertised next month. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Keep it confidential until advertised, then apply on equal terms
Start preparing from the internal planning papers while they are available
Ask the manager to hold the post open for her
Tell her friend so they can prepare, since the post will be public soon

questions.hint: Advance information would give unfair advantage; it should wait for the advert.

questions.prompt: A manager writing the criteria for a post knows one colleague well and shapes the essential criteria to match the colleague's experience. What is wrong?

options.text: The criteria should have been shorter and less specific
The criteria are tailored to a person, which is unfair
The criteria are too detailed for an advert at this grade
Nothing is wrong, since the manager knows the work best

questions.hint: Criteria must reflect the job, not the person.

questions.prompt: Which is a misuse of panel membership?

options.text: Declaring a relationship with a candidate before shortlisting
Discussing candidates informally outside the process
Scoring each answer against the published criteria
Recording the reasons for each score awarded

questions.hint: Confidentiality of the process must be maintained.

questions.prompt: A panel member knows from other work that a candidate is excellent, though the application does not show it. What is the best approach?

options.text: Declare it and let the chair decide how to proceed
Ask the candidate to add the point to the application
Use it quietly to raise the candidate's score
Say nothing and score on the application alone

questions.hint: Hidden knowledge undermines equal treatment, so declare it.

questions.prompt: After a competition, a colleague asks the panel member why a friend was unsuccessful. What should she do?

options.text: Tell the colleague's own manager what was said
Share the scores, as the colleague is a friend of the candidate
Decline to share notes and point to the feedback route
Share general impressions only, leaving out the scores

questions.hint: Results and notes are confidential, and feedback goes through the process.

questions.prompt: Why do these rules protect individuals, as well as the Service?

options.text: They shorten the process for every candidate who applies to the department
They guarantee that panel members will be promoted for acting fairly
They reduce the number of candidates who put themselves forward for posts
Unfair advantage can lead to challenge and disciplinary action

questions.hint: Challenge and discipline are real risks.

questions.prompt: Which is an acceptable use of knowledge gained in your current role?

options.text: Using colleagues' performance ratings to compare yourself with them
Using your own work achievements as evidence
Using confidential costings from the restructure to write a strategic answer
Using unpublished plans to anticipate the interview questions

questions.hint: Your own achievements are legitimate evidence; confidential material is not.

questions.prompt: When in doubt about whether an action is proper, what should a civil servant do?

options.text: Ask a friend in another department what they would do
Do nothing for as long as the doubt remains
Act first, and explain afterwards if challenged
Ask HR or a nominated officer before acting

questions.hint: Seeking advice first is the safe route.

questions.prompt: Which Civil Service Code value is most directly engaged by using unpublished information for personal gain?

options.text: Efficiency, since the information speeds up the work of the post
Seniority, since senior staff are entitled to advance knowledge
Integrity, since information is being used for personal gain
Speed, since the information allows an earlier application

questions.hint: Misuse of information is a breach of integrity.

questions.prompt: A candidate learns confidential information about the interview format through a friend on the panel. What is the right action?

options.text: Not use it, and tell the department what happened
Use it, since the candidate did not seek it out
Ask the friend for more detail to check it is accurate
Share it with other candidates to keep things level

questions.hint: Using or spreading it would undermine fairness.

items.title: L10: When acting-up turns into a de facto promotion
items.source: Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: Managers face real pressure to keep work moving, and one way is to ask a capable person to act up into a vacant higher post. That is often sensible and develops the person. The problem arises when an arrangement meant to be temporary becomes long-term without a fair competition, because the person gains recent experience, a track record and a seat on the team, which makes them the obvious candidate later. Other eligible staff never had the chance. Under the Recruitment Principles, permanent promotion must follow a fair and open competition, and departments are expected to manage temporary arrangements so that they do not become a back door. Good practice includes a clear end date, a record of why this person was chosen, a fair process for selecting the person where the arrangement is likely to be long, a review at set intervals, and early advertising of the permanent post. If the person wins the later competition on merit, that is fine, but the competition must be genuine, and the panel should consider the evidence presented rather than assuming the acting person is the best. As a manager facing this, consider the effect on the team and on candidates who were not offered the chance. As an acting person, be aware that you are not entitled to the post, and keep your evidence ready to compete. As a colleague who is concerned, you can raise it with the manager, HR, or the nominated officer, and ultimately the Commission.

questions.prompt: Why does a long acting-up arrangement raise a fairness concern?

options.text: It prevents other staff from applying for any posts
It means the permanent post can never be advertised
It gives one person experience others never had
It reduces the pay costs of the department

questions.hint: The advantage affects the later competition.

questions.prompt: A manager has an acting arrangement that is likely to last 15 months. What is the best practice?

options.text: Appoint the person permanently without a competition
Ask the person already in the room to continue indefinitely
Extend the arrangement quietly every three months
Select fairly and advertise the permanent post early

questions.hint: Longer arrangements need a fair process and planning.

questions.prompt: Which is a sound management practice for acting-up?

options.text: A clear end date and a recorded reason
An open-ended arrangement with no end date
A verbal agreement only, to keep things flexible
A promise of the permanent post to the acting person

questions.hint: Clarity and records make the process defensible.

questions.prompt: The acting person later applies for the permanent post. What should the panel do?

options.text: Assume they are best because of the time spent acting up
Assess the evidence against the criteria, as for every candidate
Exclude them because the arrangement gave them an advantage
Appoint them without an interview as they are already doing the job

questions.prompt: What is the right attitude for the acting person?

options.text: Ask to be appointed straight away to avoid a competition
Assume the post will be theirs once the arrangement ends
Refuse to apply, to avoid any appearance of conflict
Know there is no entitlement, and keep evidence ready

questions.hint: Acting up gives experience, not a right.

questions.prompt: How might a colleague who is concerned about an acting arrangement proceed?

options.text: Refuse to work with the acting person until the matter is settled
Share it widely among colleagues so that others can judge it
Raise it with the manager, HR or a nominated officer first
Complain publicly about the arrangement on an open forum

questions.prompt: What does a manager need to consider besides the work pressure?

options.text: The cost of advertising the permanent post to the public
The effect on the team and on staff not offered the chance
The popularity of the acting person with the rest of the team
The wishes of the acting person, who has the most to gain

questions.hint: Fairness to others is part of the decision.

questions.prompt: How should an acting person who wins the later competition on merit be viewed?

options.text: Acceptable if the competition is genuine and won on merit
It is wrong, since the acting person had an advantage
It is wrong whenever the winner is already internal
It is wrong, since acting up is itself a form of promotion

questions.hint: A genuine merit win is acceptable.

questions.prompt: What is a 'back door' in this context?

options.text: A form of loan arranged between two departments
A secure staff entrance used by managers outside office hours
A route to promotion that avoids fair competition
A reserve list used for staff whose own posts have closed

questions.prompt: Which action would best reduce the risk of the arrangement becoming a de facto promotion?

options.text: Advertise the post early and review at set intervals
Ending the arrangement without notice to the person
Keeping the arrangement secret from the rest of the team
Ignoring the end date when it arrives

questions.hint: Early advertising and reviews keep the process honest.

items.title: L10: Running a fair and consistent sift
items.source: Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: For those who help to run recruitment, the quality of the sift determines the fairness of everything that follows. Good practice begins before applications arrive: agree the criteria and scoring scale, with descriptors that say what each score looks like, and decide how many candidates will progress. Brief all markers, using example answers, and run a calibration session in which each marker scores the same sample and the group discusses differences. Where possible, anonymise applications by removing names and personal details, so that marking responds to the evidence rather than to assumptions. Markers should score each answer independently, against the scale, and record brief reasons. Do not compare candidates against each other before applying the scale. Moderation follows: a second marker reviews a sample, and any large differences are discussed and resolved with reasons recorded. Watch for known bias patterns: preferring answers in a familiar style, marking down unfamiliar organisations, and being swayed by an excellent answer to one question when scoring others. Handle borderline cases consistently, with a rule agreed in advance. Keep records, because candidates may ask for feedback, and the department may need to explain decisions. Check that adjustments requested by candidates have been applied, for example where a word limit was relaxed. Finally, review outcomes for any unexplained patterns by group, which may point to a problem in the criteria or marking. A fair sift is consistent, documented and open to challenge.

questions.prompt: Why run a calibration session before sifting?

options.text: To shorten the sift by reducing the number of answers read
So markers score a sample and agree the scale
To raise the pass mark before the real marking begins
So each marker can adopt a favoured style of answer

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of anonymising applications?

options.text: To hide scores from the panel at the end
To make the sift faster for the markers
To keep candidates unknown to the department for ever
To reduce the influence of assumptions about names

questions.prompt: Which is an example of halo-effect bias in a sift?

options.text: Recording reasons for each score in the marker's notes
Being swayed by one excellent answer elsewhere
Using a second marker to review a sample of the answers
Scoring every answer against the scale before comparing them

questions.hint: Halo effects let one strong impression colour the rest.

questions.prompt: A marker prefers answers in a familiar organisational style and marks down others. What is the problem?

options.text: Marking is responding to style, not evidence
The marker is recording reasons that are too detailed
The marker is being too consistent in applying the scale
The marker is applying the scale as it was intended

questions.hint: Evidence should be scored, not familiarity.

questions.prompt: What does moderation involve?

options.text: The chair raises every score so that no candidate is marked harshly
Candidates review each other's answers to check the marking
The hiring manager chooses the candidates after the markers finish
A second marker reviews a sample and differences are resolved

questions.prompt: Why should markers not compare candidates with each other before applying the scale?

options.text: It makes the sift slower, with no effect on the scores
It is forbidden by law, so any comparison is unlawful in a sift
It can pull scores away from the scale's standard
It raises the scores of all of the candidates considered

questions.prompt: How should borderline cases be handled?

options.text: By the marker's judgement on the day
By a rule agreed in advance
By choosing the internal candidate where possible
By drawing lots between the candidates

questions.hint: A pre-agreed rule treats everyone alike.

questions.prompt: Why keep brief written reasons for scores?

options.text: They let decisions be explained and challenged
They shorten the time taken to give feedback to candidates
They are needed for payroll purposes when staff are appointed
They replace the numerical scores in the final report

questions.prompt: What might reviewing outcomes by group reveal?

options.text: The identities of the candidates who were successful
The private preferences of each of the panel members
The pay levels that each candidate was previously on
A pattern pointing to problems in the criteria

questions.prompt: Which candidate adjustment might a sift need to apply?

options.text: A higher score for the candidate, in compensation for the barrier
A different scale used only for that candidate's answers
A relaxed word limit or an alternative format agreed in advance
A skipped criterion that the candidate finds hard to evidence

questions.hint: Adjustments must be reflected in the marking.

items.title: L10: When a manager obstructs a move
items.source: Civil Service HR guidance; Civil Service Code
items.body: A civil servant who has been offered a new post can find that the current manager is reluctant to release them, often because of workload. Understanding the rules and the options helps you to act well. Usually, a person who has been appointed on a permanent basis is released after their notice period, and the receiving department and the home department agree a date. In some cases, especially loans, secondments and level transfers within the Civil Service, a release date is negotiated and may be later than the person would like, because business need is considered. Most departments set a maximum release period, often a few months, to prevent a person being held indefinitely. Start with a calm conversation with your manager, explaining what the post offers and proposing a handover plan. If agreement is hard, involve HR, who can advise on the policy and mediate. Keep your tone professional and record key steps in writing. Avoid ultimatums, and do not suggest that the manager's reluctance is a breach unless you have evidence, because it may be a legitimate business reason. If you believe you are being treated unfairly because you applied, for example that you are being given worse work, this may be a concern to raise through the proper route. Never take actions that would damage your relationship with the new department, such as missing agreed dates without warning. If a delay is unavoidable, keep the new line manager informed.

questions.prompt: A manager says workload means a staff member cannot be released for three months. What is typical?

options.text: A date is negotiated, balancing business need within a maximum
The staff member is released on the day the offer is accepted
The staff member must stay for as long as the manager considers necessary
The new department alone decides the date, whatever the old team needs

questions.hint: Release dates balance business need and the person's move.

questions.prompt: What is the best first step when a manager is reluctant to release you?

options.text: Contact the new manager and complain about the delay
Talk calmly, explain the post and propose a handover plan
Email the whole team to explain that she is being held back
Threaten to resign unless she is released at once

questions.hint: A constructive conversation is the first step.

questions.prompt: In what circumstances is HR most useful in a disputed release?

options.text: Paying the person to stay in the post for longer
Changing the release date on its own authority
Advising on policy and mediating if agreement is hard
Blocking the move until the team has recruited a replacement

questions.prompt: Which action is unhelpful?

options.text: Proposing a handover plan to cover the outstanding work
Keeping a written record of the key steps in the discussion
Involving HR if agreement turns out to be hard to reach
Issuing an ultimatum to release you immediately

questions.prompt: How should you treat a manager's reluctance to release you?

options.text: Not without evidence, as there may be a legitimate business reason
As a breach whenever the new post is a promotion
As a breach, since a manager must release any member of staff who is appointed
As a breach whenever the manager is senior to the person

questions.hint: Business need can be a valid reason.

questions.prompt: Rob believes he is being given worse work after applying for a post. How should he act?

options.text: Complain about the manager on a social media account
Withdraw the application so that the treatment stops
Raise it through the proper route, such as HR
Quietly accept it and say nothing, to avoid making matters worse

questions.hint: Concerns about unfair treatment can be raised properly.

questions.prompt: What should a candidate do if a delay in release is unavoidable?

options.text: Tell the new department that the old manager is blocking the move
Keep the new line manager informed of the position
Accept any delay without telling anybody outside the team
Avoid contacting the new department until the date is certain

questions.prompt: Which behaviour could damage the relationship with the new department?

options.text: Offering a handover plan for the outstanding work
Confirming the start date once it has been agreed
Providing regular updates on progress
Missing agreed dates without warning

questions.prompt: Why do departments often set a maximum release period?

options.text: To stop a person being held indefinitely
To discourage transfers between departments
To save pay costs for the receiving department
To cap the number of applications a person can make

questions.hint: A cap protects the person's move.

questions.prompt: Which statement about release after appointment is most accurate?

options.text: The person can be held in post for up to a year
The person has no right to be released at all
Release usually follows the notice period and an agreed date
The person can leave on the same day as the offer is accepted

items.title: L10: Persistence, setbacks and when to change approach
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Persistence is valuable, but only if it is paired with learning. After a run of rejections, a useful discipline is to separate three questions: is the target right, is the evidence strong enough, and is the delivery good enough? If the target is wrong, for example the grade is above your evidence or the profession does not fit, changing it is wise, not defeatist. If the evidence is not strong enough, build it through projects, loans or a different role, and apply again once you have it. If delivery is the problem, practise writing and interviewing with feedback. Set a review point, such as after six applications, to examine outcomes against these questions. Avoid two traps. One is to keep repeating the same approach hoping for a different result. The other is to change everything after every rejection, so that you never learn which change helped. Look at the evidence honestly: if scores are close to the pass mark, persist with refinement; if they are far below, alter the strategy. Manage your wellbeing, because repeated rejection can affect confidence. Talk to people who can help, such as a mentor, a colleague or a support network, and keep other parts of your life going. Decide in advance what would make you step back, such as a set number of unsuccessful applications, and what you would do then, such as a focused development period. Persistence includes knowing when to pause.

questions.prompt: After a run of rejections, which three questions help to diagnose the problem?

options.text: Is the panel fair, is the system working, and is the advert accurate
Is the target right, is the evidence strong, and is the delivery good
Is the salary right, is the location right, and is the manager suitable
Is the date right, is the closing time right, and is the stage order right

questions.hint: Separating these questions guides the response.

questions.prompt: If the target is wrong, such as a grade above your evidence, what is wise?

options.text: Keep applying to the same roles in case the field changes
Apply to even higher grades to make a stronger point
Stop applying for any role for at least a year
Change the target, since that is not defeatist

questions.prompt: If the evidence is not strong enough, what should you do?

options.text: Exaggerate the examples so that they score higher
Build it through projects, loans or another role
Ask the department to raise the sift scores
Reword the same evidence in a different order

questions.prompt: Which trap does repeating the same approach hoping for a different result represent?

options.text: A sign of resilience that should be encouraged
A rule that Civil Service Jobs applies to repeat applicants
Failing to learn from outcomes
A recommended approach after any rejection

questions.prompt: Which trap does changing everything after every rejection represent?

options.text: Never learning which change helped
A rule that Civil Service Jobs applies to repeat applicants
A way of guaranteeing eventual success
Excellent adaptability that markers reward

questions.hint: Change one thing at a time.

questions.prompt: Scores sit just under the pass mark across several attempts. What does this suggest?

options.text: Abandon the strategy altogether at this point
Challenge the panel's scoring in writing
Change profession immediately without reviewing
Keep going, refining the evidence

questions.hint: Close scores imply a narrow gap.

questions.prompt: If every score is well short of the pass mark over several attempts, what does that point to?

options.text: Apply for the same roles more quickly
Complain that the scoring scale is unfair
Change the target or the evidence
Persist with exactly the same approach

questions.hint: Large gaps need a different approach.

questions.prompt: Why set a review point, such as after six applications?

options.text: To submit more applications each week to improve the odds
To check outcomes against the three questions
To compare results with those of other candidates
To stop applying altogether once six have been made

questions.prompt: Why decide in advance what would make you step back?

options.text: It prevents drifting and lets you plan a development period
It guarantees a result by the end of the period
It is required by HR for people who have been rejected repeatedly
It reduces the pay on offer in future roles

questions.prompt: Which is a sensible way to protect wellbeing during a long search?

options.text: Work longer hours until a result finally arrives
Apply to more roles each week to rebuild confidence
Avoid feedback altogether so that it cannot affect confidence
Talk to a mentor and keep other parts of life going

items.title: L10: Long-term career planning across professions and grades
items.source: GOV.UK, Civil Service Professions and Functions; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: A career in the Civil Service can be planned in terms of grade, profession and breadth. Grades give a ladder of responsibility, from AA and AO through EO, HEO, SEO, Grade 7 and Grade 6 to the Senior Civil Service. Professions, such as policy, operational delivery, digital and data, finance, analysis and commercial, give a pathway of specialist skills, and many publish frameworks for the skills expected at each grade. Breadth is the range of experiences in different teams, departments and types of work, which many senior roles value. A sound plan sets an ambition for three to five years, such as reaching HEO in a given profession, and then works backwards: which skills and evidence are needed, who can help, and which moves give the best chance. Within the plan, aim for a mix of depth and breadth. Depth shows mastery, and breadth shows adaptability and understanding of how the system works. Some people deliberately take a lateral move to gain breadth before seeking promotion. The plan should also allow for change: priorities, family circumstances and the structure of departments shift, so review it at least annually. Seek mentors beyond your line manager, including people in other departments and in your profession. Keep a record of achievements and learning. Treat the plan as a set of choices, not a promise, since promotion depends on vacancies, competition and merit, which you cannot control.

questions.prompt: Which sequence shows the broad order of Civil Service grades?

options.text: AO, AA, HEO, EO, Grade 6, Grade 7, SEO, Senior Civil Service
AA, EO, AO, SEO, HEO, Grade 6, Grade 7, Senior Civil Service
AA, AO, EO, HEO, SEO, Grade 7, Grade 6, Senior Civil Service
EO, AO, AA, SEO, HEO, Grade 7, Grade 6, Senior Civil Service

questions.hint: That is the standard sequence from AA upwards.

questions.prompt: What does a professional framework describe?

options.text: The reserve lists held for the profession
The pay awarded for each post in the profession
The membership of the panel for each competition
The skills expected at each grade

questions.prompt: Why do many senior roles value breadth?

options.text: It shows adaptability
It shortens probation in the new post
It reduces the number of applications received
It guarantees a move to the next higher grade

questions.prompt: How should an ambition be turned into a plan?

options.text: Wait for a manager to decide the next step
Work backwards to the skills and moves needed
Apply for every vacancy that appears, whatever the role
Copy a colleague's route exactly, step by step

questions.hint: A plan works backwards from the goal.

questions.prompt: Why might someone take a lateral move before seeking promotion?

options.text: To avoid being assessed in a competition
To gain breadth for later applications
To increase their pay straight away
To reduce their responsibility for a period

questions.hint: Breadth can be a deliberate step.

questions.prompt: How often should a career plan be reviewed?

options.text: At least annually, as circumstances change
Never, so that the plan stays fixed
Only when a suitable vacancy is advertised
Only after a promotion has been won

questions.prompt: Whom should you seek as mentors?

options.text: Only your line manager, who knows your work best
Only people in your own team, who share your context
People beyond your line manager, in other departments
Only people at your own grade, who face the same issues

questions.hint: A wider range gives better advice.

questions.prompt: Why treat a career plan as choices rather than a promise?

options.text: Career plans are against Civil Service rules
Career plans cannot name specific grades
Career plans must be approved by HR before they are used
Promotion depends on vacancies, competition and merit

questions.prompt: Which pair shows a balance of depth and breadth?

options.text: Many very short roles with no real depth in any
One role held for twenty years in the same team
Mastery in one profession plus varied teams
A series of identical posts in separate departments

questions.prompt: What should accompany a career plan?

options.text: A record of achievements and learning
A copy of the latest advert in the profession
A list of the vacancies that were rejected
A letter of support from a former panel

items.title: L10: Designing criteria without indirect discrimination
items.source: Equality Act 2010; EHRC, Employment statutory code of practice
items.body: People who write job descriptions and person specifications can unintentionally create indirect discrimination. A provision, criterion or practice is indirectly discriminatory if it applies to everyone but puts people who share a protected characteristic at a particular disadvantage, puts the person at that disadvantage, and cannot be shown to be a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. Examples to watch for include requirements for a specific number of years of continuous service, which can disadvantage people who have taken career breaks; requirements for a degree where equivalent experience would show the same ability; rigid hours or location requirements that are not needed for the work; and tests that depend on knowledge more likely to be held by one group. To avoid the problem, start from what the job genuinely requires, and describe it in terms of outcomes and ability rather than length of service or specific routes. Distinguish essential from desirable criteria: if something can be learned in post, it should not be essential. Consider whether a requirement is necessary and whether a less discriminatory alternative would meet the same aim. If a criterion is retained because it is necessary, record the reason. Test the draft with a diverse group, and review data on who applies and who succeeds. Where a criterion is challenged, be ready to explain what legitimate aim it serves and why it is proportionate. Remember that a legitimate aim is a real business need, not mere convenience.

questions.prompt: Which criterion is most likely to create indirect discrimination?

options.text: 'Right to work in the UK, checked before appointment'
'Willingness to work as part of a team on shared tasks'
'Ability to analyse data and write clear advice for ministers'
'Five years of continuous, uninterrupted service'

questions.hint: Continuous service can disadvantage people with career breaks.

questions.prompt: What must an employer show to defend a provision that puts a group at a disadvantage?

options.text: That most candidates accept it when they apply
That it is proportionate and serves a legitimate aim
That it has been used in the department for many years
That it is cheaper to apply than the alternatives

questions.hint: Proportionality and a legitimate aim are required.

questions.prompt: Which is a better way to describe a requirement?

options.text: In terms of age bands that suit each grade
In terms of outcomes and ability needed, not length of service
In terms of how long the person has worked in total
In terms of specific previous employers a person has worked for

questions.prompt: Why avoid listing as essential something that can be learned in post?

options.text: It is required by law for all adverts
It makes the advert shorter and simpler to read
It may needlessly exclude capable candidates
It makes the sift faster for the markers

questions.hint: Essential criteria should be limited to what is needed at the start.

questions.prompt: What does a degree requirement need to be justified by?

options.text: The personal preference of the hiring manager
Tradition in the department about who has done the job
The number of applicants likely to apply
A genuine need equivalent experience could not meet

questions.prompt: Which of these is a legitimate aim?

options.text: A real business need, such as safety
A wish to reduce the number of applications received
A preference for candidates the panel already knows
Mere convenience for the manager who runs the team

questions.prompt: How can a draft person specification be tested?

options.text: By comparing it with the last advert for the same post
With a diverse group, and by reviewing outcome data
By asking only the hiring manager what they think
By publishing it without further review

questions.prompt: If a criterion is retained as necessary, what is good practice?

options.text: Record the reason for it
Apply it to some candidates only
Remove it from the advert
Keep it secret from candidates

questions.prompt: Why might rigid hours or location requirements be risky?

options.text: They are unlawful in every case, whatever the reason
They always reduce the number of applications received
They can disadvantage some groups if not needed
They make adverts longer and harder for candidates to read

questions.prompt: Which question should be asked about a requirement?

options.text: Is it popular with the people who currently do the job?
Is it cheap to apply and easy to mark?
Is it traditional, and has it been used in earlier campaigns?
Is it necessary, and is there a less harmful alternative?

items.title: L10: The limits of the duty to adjust
items.source: Equality Act 2010; EHRC, Employment statutory code of practice
items.body: The duty to make reasonable adjustments is strong, but it has limits, and judging them is a skill. The duty arises where a provision, criterion or practice, a physical feature, or the lack of an auxiliary aid puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage compared with people who are not disabled. It applies in recruitment and in employment, and an employer is expected to act if it knows, or could reasonably be expected to know, that a person is disabled and likely to be disadvantaged. The measure of reasonableness is objective. Relevant factors include whether the step would be effective in removing the disadvantage, how practicable it is, the cost, the resources and size of the organisation, any disruption it would cause, and whether outside financial help is available, such as Access to Work. A large department is expected to bear significant costs. An adjustment is not reasonable if it would not be effective, even if it is easy and cheap. An employer cannot require the person to pay for an adjustment. The duty does not require the removal of an essential part of the job, but it may require a change in how it is done, for example through equipment or a different method. Consultation matters: discuss the options with the person, because they usually know what works. Review adjustments periodically, as needs and technology change. Failure to make a reasonable adjustment is itself a form of discrimination and does not require a comparison with another person.

questions.prompt: Which question determines whether an adjustment is reasonable?

options.text: Whether it is effective and practicable
Whether other staff would also like to have it
Whether it was used for a previous candidate last year
Whether the person asked for it politely

questions.prompt: Where an adjustment is cheap but would not remove the disadvantage, how is it judged?

options.text: It is reasonable, because cost is the only thing that matters
It is reasonable, because it shows the employer tried
It is not reasonable, because an adjustment must be effective
It is reasonable, if the person asks for it

questions.prompt: Who bears the cost of a reasonable adjustment?

options.text: The disabled person, unless they receive outside funding
The employer, which cannot make the person pay
The other members of staff in the team
The Civil Service Commission, which holds a central fund

questions.prompt: What could Access to Work affect?

options.text: The score given at the sift for the person's application
The pay the person is awarded when they are first appointed
The grade given to the post after job evaluation is done
Outside funding, which is a factor in reasonableness

questions.prompt: What does the duty to adjust require where a task is an essential part of the job?

options.text: It requires removal in every case, whatever the effect
It requires removal whenever the cost is high enough
It may require changing how the work is done
It requires removal whenever the person asks for it

questions.hint: The core remains; the method may change.

questions.prompt: Why consult the person about options?

options.text: It reduces the cost of the adjustment to zero
It delays the process, and allows the department to think
It guarantees that the request will be accepted
They usually know what works for them

questions.prompt: Why review adjustments periodically?

options.text: Needs and technology change
Adjustments expire after a year
Reviews are required for every employee
Reviews reduce the cost of adjustments

questions.prompt: How is failure to make a reasonable adjustment treated?

options.text: As a matter for HR alone to settle informally
Discrimination in itself, with no comparison
As a minor administrative error with no consequence
As a reason for the department to reject the claim

questions.prompt: When is an employer expected to act?

options.text: Only when the person has put a complaint in writing
Only if the line manager agrees to it
When it knows, or should know, of the disadvantage
Only after the person's probation has been completed

questions.hint: Knowledge, actual or constructive, triggers the duty.

questions.prompt: Which factor increases what is expected of a large department?

options.text: Its location in the country
Its age as an organisation
Its public profile
Its size and resources

questions.hint: Larger organisations are expected to do more.

items.title: L10: Equal merit and difficult panel decisions
items.source: Equality Act 2010, section 159; Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles
items.body: Panels sometimes face a close call between two strong candidates. The first step is to be sure that the scores really are equal on the evidence, because pretending to be equal to apply a preference is not allowed. Review the notes for each candidate against the criteria, and check that no stray factors, such as familiarity or style, have crept in. If the candidates are genuinely equal on merit, the panel may use a tie-break that is lawful and fair. The Equality Act allows a preference for a candidate with a protected characteristic in limited circumstances, where the organisation reasonably believes that people with that characteristic are disadvantaged or under-represented, where the candidates are as qualified as one another, and where the step is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. It cannot be applied as a blanket policy, and each case must be considered on its own facts, taking account of all relevant circumstances. Departments often adopt a published approach, so the panel should follow the department's guidance and record the reasons. Other tie-break approaches include looking again at the lead behaviour or at an agreed additional criterion, if one was set in advance. A panel should not choose on personal liking, or by which candidate is more convenient. If the process has more candidates who pass than posts, a reserve list can help. After the decision, offer feedback to both candidates, and be ready to explain the reasoning.

questions.prompt: Before using any tie-break, what must a panel first check?

options.text: That they are genuinely equal on the evidence
That the chair prefers one of the two candidates
That both candidates are the same age and grade
That one of the candidates is already an internal one

questions.hint: A tie-break applies only to genuine equality.

questions.prompt: Which stray factor may distort a panel's view of two candidates?

options.text: A written score recorded against a criterion
Familiarity or a preferred style of answer
A reason recorded in the notes
The published scoring scale

questions.hint: Hidden bias can mimic a tie.

questions.prompt: Under the Equality Act, when may a panel prefer a candidate with a protected characteristic?

options.text: Whenever one candidate scored slightly lower than the other
Whenever the candidate asks the panel for such a preference
As qualified, group under-represented, and proportionate
Whenever the panel members would like to favour one candidate

questions.prompt: Why can the preference not be a blanket policy?

options.text: Each case must be considered on its own facts
It would slow the process down unreasonably for the panel
It would reduce the number of people who apply at all
Policies of this kind are unlawful in the Civil Service

questions.prompt: Which tie-break is acceptable if set in advance?

options.text: Choosing the candidate who is more convenient for the team
Choosing the candidate who applied earlier
Choosing the candidate the panel likes more
Revisiting the lead behaviour or an agreed criterion

questions.prompt: Which is not an acceptable reason to choose between equal candidates?

options.text: A criterion that was agreed in advance
Personal liking
A lawful and proportionate preference
A published approach from the department

questions.prompt: What helps if more candidates pass than there are posts?

options.text: A new competition for the same post
A reserve list
Extending the number of posts
Removing candidates at random

questions.prompt: What should happen after a close panel decision has been made?

options.text: Feedback is offered to both and reasons explained
Feedback is refused to the unsuccessful candidate
Scores are published to all staff in the department
Results are kept secret from all of the candidates

questions.prompt: Why record reasons for a close decision?

options.text: To shorten the notes that the panel is required to keep
To reduce the time that the decision takes the panel
To avoid having to ask HR for advice on the process
To show it was fair, and support feedback

questions.prompt: What guidance should the panel follow on tie-breaks?

options.text: The chair's personal preference
Whatever is quickest to apply
The department's published approach
The view of the most senior panel member

items.title: L10: False claims, misconduct and consequences
items.source: Civil Service Code; Fraud Act 2006; Cabinet Office, Baseline Personnel Security Standard
items.body: Honesty in recruitment is not only a matter of good manners. The Civil Service Code requires honesty, and the pre-employment checks exist to verify claims. A candidate who gives false information about qualifications, experience, identity or right to work risks serious consequences. If discovered before appointment, the offer is likely to be withdrawn. If discovered after appointment, it may be treated as gross misconduct leading to dismissal, and the person may lose the job and face difficulty finding future public service roles. In some cases a false claim can be a criminal matter, for example fraud by false representation, and the department may refer it to the police. Not every inaccuracy is dishonest. A genuine mistake that is promptly corrected is treated differently from a deliberate attempt to deceive. Departments distinguish between embellishment, such as claiming responsibility for a team's work, and fabrication, such as a degree that does not exist. Both can be serious, but fabrication is clearer. Other forms of misconduct in the process include cheating in tests, using another person to take an online test, sharing test content, and attempting to influence panel members improperly. Departments may disqualify a candidate and note the matter. If you discover that a colleague has given false information, do not ignore it. The Code expects you to report concerns through the appropriate route, such as your line manager, HR or the nominated officer, and protections exist for those who raise concerns in good faith.

questions.prompt: What is the likely outcome if false information is found before a candidate starts?

options.text: The candidate is moved to a lower grade
The candidate receives a warning and still starts
Nothing happens if the score was high
The offer is likely to be withdrawn

questions.prompt: What might happen if a falsified degree is discovered after appointment?

options.text: The person is asked to resubmit the degree certificate
The person is given a formal written warning only
It may be gross misconduct and a criminal matter
The person is moved to another team while it is checked

questions.prompt: Which of these is fabrication rather than embellishment?

options.text: Claiming a degree that does not exist
Describing an average result as excellent
Taking credit for the team's work
Overstating the importance of a task

questions.prompt: How are genuine mistakes treated compared with deliberate deception?

options.text: They are always punished by withdrawal of the offer or dismissal
A prompt, genuine correction is treated differently
They are always ignored if the candidate scored highly
They are treated in exactly the same way by the department

questions.prompt: Which is a form of misconduct in the process?

options.text: Practising with the published sample tests before the real one
Asking the department about adjustments for a test
Requesting feedback on the test result after the campaign
Using another person to take an online test

questions.prompt: Which is also misconduct?

options.text: Preparing from the published sample questions provided
Reading the advert carefully before applying for the post
Sharing test content with other candidates
Asking the contact about the closing date of the campaign

questions.prompt: What might a department do with a candidate who cheats?

options.text: Give them extra time to finish
Disqualify them and note the matter
Offer them the job anyway
Ask them to retake the test as normal

questions.prompt: You discover that a colleague gave false information when applying. What does the Code expect?

options.text: Report it through the appropriate route
Tell other colleagues so that they can be on guard
Confront the colleague publicly in front of the team
Ignore it, as it is not something that affects you

questions.prompt: Who may you report a concern to?

options.text: A line manager, HR or the nominated officer
The family of the colleague who gave false information
Only the person who gave the false information
A newspaper that is interested in government stories

questions.prompt: Which statement about reporting concerns in good faith is true?

options.text: People who raise concerns are always dismissed
Good-faith reporting is protected
Concerns can only be raised by managers
Concerns must be proven before they can be raised

items.title: L10: Raising concerns about a recruitment process
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998; Civil Service Commission
items.body: If you are involved in or become aware of a recruitment process that you think is improper, the Civil Service Code sets out what to do. A concern may be about conflicts of interest, an appointment made without competition where one was required, criteria shaped for a person, pressure on panel members or leaked questions. First, consider whether you have the facts. Write down what you saw or were told, with dates, and distinguish what you know from what you suspect. Second, consider the appropriate route. In most cases, raise the concern with your line manager or another senior manager, or with a nominated officer, who is responsible for handling concerns under the Code. Third, if you are not satisfied, or if the concern involves your line management, you may raise it with the Civil Service Commission, which is independent and can consider concerns about breaches of the Recruitment Principles or the Code. The Public Interest Disclosure Act provides legal protection for workers who make certain disclosures in the public interest, and the Code says that civil servants should not suffer for raising concerns in good faith. Confidentiality should be respected in how the concern is handled. Avoid discussing the matter widely, and do not investigate on your own in ways that breach confidentiality or the law. Keep a record of what you report and the response. If you are a manager who receives a concern, take it seriously, protect the person who raised it and follow up. Retaliation against someone who raised a concern is a serious breach.

questions.prompt: Which is a first step if you think a process is improper?

options.text: Tell everyone in the office what you suspect has happened
Confront the panel chair in public about what you saw
Delete related emails so they cannot cause further disputes
Record facts and dates, separating fact from suspicion

questions.prompt: To whom can you usually raise a concern initially?

options.text: A competitor of the department, who may be interested
A candidate's family, who are affected by the result
Your line manager, a senior manager or nominated officer
A newspaper that regularly covers stories about government

questions.prompt: When may you go to the Civil Service Commission?

options.text: Never, as it deals only with matters outside the department
If you are unsatisfied, or your line manager is involved
Only if the vacancy was advertised externally
Only after a full year has passed since the competition

questions.hint: The Commission is an independent route.

questions.prompt: What does the Public Interest Disclosure Act provide?

options.text: Legal protection for public interest disclosures
A guarantee of promotion
Pay for people who blow the whistle
A right to choose the panel

questions.prompt: What does the Code say about those who raise concerns in good faith?

options.text: They should be named publicly
They should be moved to another team
They should be asked to withdraw it
They should not suffer for doing so

questions.prompt: Which action is wrong when raising a concern?

options.text: Keeping a record of what you report
Distinguishing fact from suspicion
Investigating alone and breaching confidentiality
Raising it through the proper route

questions.prompt: How should a manager who receives a concern respond?

options.text: Dismiss it, as most concerns are not serious
Delay action for a year in case it fades
Tell the person concerned who made the complaint
Take it seriously and protect the person

questions.prompt: What is a serious breach?

options.text: Offering support to the person who raised the concern
Recording the concern in writing, with the date and facts
Retaliation against the person who raised a concern
Following the concern up with the person who raised it

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a concern about recruitment?

options.text: A feedback email sent to a candidate after the sift
Questions leaked to a favoured candidate
A recorded score with reasons set out beside it
A published advert that states the closing date

questions.prompt: Why keep a record of what you report and the response?

options.text: It supports any later review
It is required for payroll when the person is appointed
It replaces the need for a formal written report
It reduces the time taken to deal with the concern
